name: Baka
overview: A minority, mobile and egalitarian forest people, the Baka live alongside the Nzimé and the Mpoupieng, from Yokadouma to Lomié and as far as Bipindi. Hunting, gathering, fishing and small-scale farming sustain a community where land is a common good and where the jengi initiates ensure justice and protection.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority but homogeneous group, integrated with the Nzimé and the Mpoupieng, whose language it also speaks.
Baka is spoken in Yokadouma, Lomié, Moloundou, Lolodorf and Bipindi.
The name Baka evokes the freedom of a mobile people; their neighbours call them Ibayaka. The administrative term “Pygmy” is an external designation.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Baka arrived from the Yokadouma region with the Mpoupieng, passing through Lomié and Mindourou.
They maintain ties of economic exchange and clientship with their neighbours.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Prestige comes from hunting: having killed an elephant, a gorilla, a chimpanzee or a wild boar.
Decisions are taken as a group, after consultation of the notables: the hunter, the senior woman and the healer.
Societies of initiates (Edjengui, Mokondji, Ebouadaka, Moyobe), renewed through trials, ensure justice, protection and stability.
Avoidance: the son-in-law avoids his mother-in-law. Caution: one does not go into the bush alone, nor during mourning.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Marriage mostly endogamous; when there is exogamy, it is mostly women who marry Nzimé or Mpoupieng.
Patrilineal kinship; the husband lives with his wife until the bride price is paid.
The reported ages at marriage are early.
Marriage begins with an informal meeting of the young people, each informs their parents, then the young man joins the young woman: this is the start of the bride price.
Rather than in goods, the bride price is paid in labour: the husband works for about three years to feed his in-laws.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The jengi (ndjengui) rite, celebrated according to the elders' decision, brings together the spirits and the population.
Sacred places: the sacred forest and the large village courtyard, linked to animal species.
Komba, the Creator, sends the children; death is a separation and a return to Komba. No relationship is kept up with the dead.
Food taboos: eating certain animals exposes one to serious illness.
Selfishness is the capital offence: Komba then sends bad luck.
Divination: clairvoyance and the use of wild cat skins (wildcat, civet, panther).

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: hunting, gathering, farming. Women: farming, fishing, gathering.
The land belongs to the whole group: it is a communal asset.
Ancestral basketry crafts: mats, baskets, carrying baskets, hampers.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Traditional medicine is reputed to be effective and less costly.
Beauty is not physical: it is behaviour that counts, for men as for women.
Courtship: kindness, simplicity and hard work.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms and dances: ngangan during divination, ebouma for mourning and funerals, essongo in times of joy.
Instruments: tam-tam and drum.
Festivals: jengi and beka.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The history of the Baka joins that of the other forest peoples of Cameroon and Central Africa; their relations with their neighbours deserve in-depth study.

sections.title: The names
items: No particular structure: the name is chosen in family consultation and does not change.
Nicknames linked to a person's activity are numerous.
Each clan bears the name of its ancestor, preceded by yé or di (“descendant of”).

lessons.title: Who are the Baka? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Baka community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Baka community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Baka community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Baka community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Baka community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Baka call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Minority but homogeneous group, integrated with the Nzimé and the Mpoupieng, whose language it also speaks. • Baka is spoken at Yokadouma, Lomié, Moloundou, Lolodorf and Bipindi. • The name Baka evokes the freedom of a mobile people; their neighbours call them Ibayaka. The administrative term “Pygmy” is an outside designation. • The Baka arrived from the Yokadouma region with the Mpoupieng, passing through Lomié and Mindourou. • They maintain ties of economic exchange and clientship with their neighbours.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A minority, mobile and egalitarian forest people, the Baka live alongside the Nzimé and the Mpoupieng, from Yokadouma to Lomié and as far as Bipindi. Hunting, gathering, fishing and small-scale farming sustain a community where land is a common good and where the jengi initiates ensure justice and protection.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Baka community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Baka

lessons.competence: Describe how the Baka organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Baka village. Who decides, and how?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

Caution: one does not go alone into the bush, nor during mourning.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Baka
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Baka, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Baka.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Baka, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Baka.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: wild yam (sapa), wild mango (pekè), honey (poki). • Drinks: to be collected from the elders. • Men: hunting, gathering, farming. Women: farming, fishing, gathering.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Baka mainly eat wild yam, pekè, honey. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Baka: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Baka
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Baka welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Baka family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Baka welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Baka family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No particular structure: the name is chosen in family consultation and does not change. • Nicknames linked to a person's activity are numerous. • Each clan bears the name of its ancestor, preceded by yé or di (“descendant of”). • Komba, the Creator, sends the children; death is a separation and a return to Komba. No relationship is kept up with the dead. • Marriage is mostly endogamous; when there is exogamy, it is mostly women who marry Nzimé or Mpoupieng men.

steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: hunting, gathering, farming. Women: farming, fishing, gathering. • Land belongs to the whole group: it is a communal asset. • Ancestral basketry crafts: mats, baskets, carrying baskets, hampers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Baka
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Baka, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Baka. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Baka, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Baka. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The jengi (ndjengui) rite, celebrated according to the decision of the elders, brings together the spirits and the population. • Sacred places: the sacred forest and the village's great courtyard, linked to animal species. • Komba, the Creator, sends children; death is a separation and a return to Komba. No relationship is kept up with the dead. • Food taboos: eating certain animals exposes one to serious illnesses. • Selfishness is the cardinal fault: Komba then sends bad luck.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The jengi (ndjengui) rite, celebrated according to the elders' decision, brings together the spirits and the population. Sacred places: the sacred forest and the great village courtyard, linked to animal species.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Baka (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Baka
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Baka and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Baka family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Baka greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Baka family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Baka. • Greetings: Djoko = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Modjukwè = morning greeting (one person); Iya djukwè = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Mpkodé, Bidé, Mbata, Fouè, Fouè. • Each clan bears the name of its ancestor, preceded by yé or di (“descendant of”). • The history of the Baka joins that of the other forest peoples of Cameroon and Central Africa; their relations with their neighbours deserve in-depth study.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Baka are the first steps towards communicating with the Baka. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Baka.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Baka are the first steps towards communicating with the Baka. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
